$schema-note: Hand-maintained. Data, not code: nothing under src/ imports this file.
purpose: The guard ledger for WIN-258 TRANCHE 5 — `privacy`'s canonical store, the
THIRTEENTH owner behind the one PostgreSQL client ADR M0.3 §15 gives the ORM.
One entry per guard: per shape check that stands where a migration-only
constraint or a column type stands, per vocabulary check that keeps a row an
older or newer binary wrote READABLE, per scope predicate, per clause of the
compare-and-set the port requires to be one statement, and per statement the
port's contract says must NOT be sent. Each carries the file it lives in, the
EXACT text that implements it (`from`), the edit that removes it (`to`), and
the NAMED cases that were seen to go red (`kills`).
IT IS AN ELEVENTH FILE beside mutations.json, mutations-identity.json,
mutations-ports.json, mutations-outbox.json, mutations-tools.json,
mutations-agents.json, mutations-cost.json, mutations-channels.json,
mutations-governance.json, mutations-secrets.json, mutations-skills.json,
mutations-providers.json, mutations-conversations.json and
mutations-memory.json rather than an extension of any of them, for the reason
the fourth was: each tranche is a separate claim about a separate port
surface, and a reader checking one should not have to read past the others.
All are hashed by the same packages.adapters.config rule and counted together
by the v1 ledger.
WHY THIS TRANCHE NEEDED ITS OWN SWEEP, and it is the sharpest reason any of
them has had. FOUR of the guards below cannot be exercised without TWO OPEN
TRANSACTIONS at once, and the in-memory double this store is measured against
is a map in a single-threaded process that cannot lose a race at all. TWO
MORE are about a statement that must NOT be sent: the barrier's
insert-then-extend forbids a DELETE, and 'the row is there afterwards' is
satisfied by exactly the delete-then-insert the port rules out. A conformance
differential cannot see either kind, and every one of the six would have
survived a suite written only against the double.
procedure: PROVE THE SUITES GREEN FIRST. Tranche 1's first sweep reported 22 kills and
every one was VACUOUS: a context's `dist` had been cleaned, so every suite
failed to load its import and would have 'died' against any mutation at all,
including none. The driver runs each suite set UNMUTATED and refuses to sweep
unless it is green with a non-zero executed case count, and classifies a run
with no executed cases as VACUOUS rather than as a kill.
THE INTEGRATION SUITES RUN ON A REAL POSTGRESQL, in a container, on the
machine that has a daemon. `privacy-rows.test.ts` is the only suite here that
runs without one, and it is the one that reaches the mapping branches a
container suite cannot: a container only ever reads rows THIS binary wrote,
and two of the four unreadable-row branches cannot even be PLANTED, because
`ErasureOperation.status` is a PostgreSQL ENUM and `scopes` and `stores` carry
THE STORE IS REBUILT BETWEEN MUTATIONS. `pnpm test:v1-foundation` runs
`test:clean-v1`, which removes every V1 project's dist; a sweep run after a
gate sweep without rebuilding reproduces exactly the condition that made
tranche 1's first sweep report 22 vacuous kills.
result: 34 entries, 34 KILLED, 0 VACUOUS, and the 2 declared survivors survived.
Baseline 76 executed cases, green. Run on the Mac mini against a real
THE FIRST SWEEP FOUND ONE GENUINELY UNFALSIFIABLE GUARD, which is the whole
reason a sweep is worth running. M-P14 deletes the stored-scope LEVEL check
and the case that stood for it stayed GREEN — because its witness was
`{ level: "entity", organizationId }` with no `projectId`, so the NEXT clause
refused it under the SAME code and the case could not tell which clause had
fired. A guard another guard's refusal covers is a guard nothing is holding.
`privacy-rows.test.ts`'s 25th case plants a level outside the three with EVERY
id present, so only the level check can refuse it, and M-P14 now dies.
AND IT FOUND FOUR MUTATIONS THAT WERE TYPE-INVALID RATHER THAN SURVIVABLE.
The driver scored them BUILD-FAIL — nothing ran, so neither a kill nor a
survival, which is the honest classification and not a pass. `readWorkStatus`
and `readJsonArray` return narrowed types their guards produce, so deleting
the guard alone does not compile; a bare `throw error;` makes the conflict
mapping unreachable; and `[].values()` infers `never`. Each is restated above
as an edit the compiler accepts that removes the same check, and all four then
died. A mutation the compiler refuses is a mutation that has not been scored.

mutations.name: M-P01 guards: the @db.Uuid check on every identifier
mutations.from: if (!UUID.test(value)) refuse(PRIVACY_IDENTIFIER_NOT_UUID, `${label} is not a uuid`);
mutations.to: if (false) refuse(PRIVACY_IDENTIFIER_NOT_UUID, `${label} is not a uuid`);
mutations.note: `SequenceIdGenerator` in the context's own testing fixtures mints `id-0001` for every uuid the kernel is asked for and `TEST_ORGANIZATION` is `org-1`. Both are accepted by `InMemoryPrivacyRepository`, both are refused by PostgreSQL with 22P02 INSIDE the caller's transaction, and every use-case suite in the context passes with them.
kills: the id the context's own fixtures mint is refused for a @db.Uuid column
a malformed tombstone id or operationId is refused
the store refuses `id-0001` and the caller's transaction survives it

mutations.name: M-P02 guards: an Invalid Date on any timestamp(3) column
mutations.from:
if (Number.isNaN(value.getTime())) {
    refuse(PRIVACY_INSTANT_NOT_REPRESENTABLE, `${label} is not a representable instant`);
mutations.to:
if (false) {
    refuse(PRIVACY_INSTANT_NOT_REPRESENTABLE, `${label} is not a representable instant`);
mutations.note: `backoffMs` caps its exponent precisely because `2 ** 1024` is `Infinity` and `Infinity * 0` is `NaN`. This guard is what stops a caller that did not go through that rule from putting an `Invalid Date` in `nextRetryAt`, which the driver cannot serialise.
kills: an Invalid Date is refused on every instant column

mutations.name: M-P03 guards: listDueOperations' page size is a NON-NEGATIVE int32
mutations.note: The double clamps with `Math.max(0, limit)`. Prisma REVERSES the order on a negative `take` and returns rows, so the queue would re-drive the furthest FUTURE operations first with nothing failing anywhere.
kills: a negative page limit is REFUSED rather than clamped

mutations.name: M-P04 guards: a lease is a PAIR of columns or neither
mutations.note: Neither column is NOT NULL and there is no CHECK over the pair, so PostgreSQL stores a lease that names no holder — proved by a planted row in the constraints suite. `claimLease`'s free-lease predicate would then refuse every resume until an instant nobody set.
kills: half a lease is refused in both directions
a lease pair with only one half set is refused, though both columns are nullable

mutations.name: M-P05 guards: the two _json_root CHECKs, which exist only in the migrations
mutations.from: if (!Array.isArray(value)) refuse(code, `${label} must be a JSON array at its root`);
mutations.to: if (false) refuse(code, `${label} must be a JSON array at its root`);
mutations.note: `ErasureOperation_scopes_json_root` and `ErasureOperation_stores_json_root` are both `jsonb_typeof(...) = 'array'`, and both exist ONLY in the migration. The guard stands for the value that arrives through a transport boundary with the type assertion already spent.
kills: a scopes or stores value whose root is not an array is refused, per CHECK
the store refuses a scopes value whose root is not an array
the store refuses an outcomes value whose root is not an array, under a DIFFERENT code

mutations.name: M-P06 guards: the WorkStatus enum is FIVE labels, not a string
mutations.note: The column is a PostgreSQL ENUM, so a sixth label is refused by the column itself — inside the caller's transaction, which `request-erasure.ts` is also using to append the INTENT event.
kills: a workStatus outside the enum's five labels is refused
all five of the enum's labels are readable, so the refusal is not blanket
a status label this binary has never heard of is REFUSED, not cast past
the store refuses a sixth label and the caller's transaction survives it

mutations.name: M-P07 guards: retryCount is an Int4 column
mutations.note: `Int4` is narrower than `number`, and a fractional or out-of-range count reaches the driver as a value it cannot bind. Nothing in the domain clamps it on the way into `updateProgress`.
kills: a retryCount that is not a non-negative int32 is refused

mutations.name: M-P08 guards: one seal may not span two organizations
mutations.note: Unreachable from `draftTombstones`, which builds every draft from one organization — and the one shape that would make this store's scoped read-then-split UNSOUND, because the read is scoped to the first draft's organization and would classify every other tenant's alias as missing.
kills: a batch spanning two organizations is refused

mutations.name: M-P09 guards: a retention window may not end before it begins
mutations.note: There is no CHECK over the pair, so PostgreSQL stores a tombstone that has already lapsed at the instant it is written — a barrier that was never up. The transaction suite uses this refusal as its second failure injection, so the mutation ALSO takes an unrelated-looking case with it, which is the point of naming both.
kills: a retention window that ends before it begins is refused
an operation inserted beside a doomed seal does not survive either

mutations.name: M-P10 guards: fewer minted ids than drafts to seal
mutations.note: `InMemoryPrivacyRepository` `continue`s past a draft with no id, so an alias goes UNSEALED and the reported count is short with NO error. On this port that means the barrier has a hole in it exactly where the caller believes it does not.
kills: fewer minted ids than drafts is refused rather than silently dropping a row

mutations.name: M-P11 guards: a stored SCOPE's organizationId is a uuid too
mutations.note: `scopes` is JSONB, so PostgreSQL stores this happily — and `resolvePath` then produces a key naming an organization that cannot exist. The guard is about the VALUE being a tenant reference, not about the column's type, which is why deleting it leaves every other uuid guard standing.
kills: a scope whose organizationId is not a uuid is refused, though it is JSON

mutations.name: M-P12 rows: a stored WorkStatus this binary has never heard of
mutations.note: The expand/contract branch, and the one where a cast is worst. `receiptStatusFor` has four branches and a fifth label matches none of them, so a cast reports a FINISHED operation as `pending` — a receipt saying an erasure has not started when it has.
kills: a status label this binary has never heard of is REFUSED, not cast past

mutations.name: M-P13 rows: a stored scopes or stores column whose root is not an array
mutations.from:
if (!Array.isArray(value)) unreadable(UNREADABLE_JSON_ARRAY, column, "is not a JSON array");
  return value;
mutations.note: The READ side of M-P05. A CHECK the migration installs can be dropped by a later one, and `.map` on a non-array is a TypeError inside a read path rather than a reported outcome.
kills: a scopes column whose root is not an array is refused

mutations.name: M-P14 rows: a stored scope LEVEL outside the kernel's three
mutations.note: Every kernel consumer switches on the discriminant, so a stored fourth level reaches `resolvePath` and produces a key that silently addresses the wrong subtree — a cache namespace, a rate-limit bucket or an object-storage prefix for a tenant that does not exist. IT SURVIVED THE FIRST SWEEP, and the reason was the CASE rather than the guard: the original witness was `{ level: "entity", organizationId }` with no `projectId`, so the NEXT clause refused it under the SAME code and the case could not tell which clause had fired. The case named below plants a level outside the three with EVERY id present, so only this clause can refuse it.
kills: a scope level outside the kernel's three is refused EVEN WHEN every id it would need is present

mutations.name: M-P15 rows: a stored scope missing the id its level requires
mutations.note: A `project` scope with no `projectId` is read as `undefined` inside a template string, which produces the key `org/x/proj/undefined` and no error anywhere.
kills: a project scope with no projectId is refused, and so is an environment scope with no environmentId

mutations.name: M-P16 rows: a stored target outcome with no target NAME
mutations.note: `mergeOutcomes` and `targetsNeedingRetry` both KEY on `target`, so an outcome without one silently collapses into whichever other outcome shares its `undefined` — and a retry then re-runs the wrong target or skips one that never reported.
kills: a stores element with no target name is refused

mutations.name: M-P17 operations: findOperation's ORGANIZATION predicate
mutations.from:
const row = (await transactions.reader().erasureOperation.findFirst({
          where: { id: operationId, organizationId },
mutations.note: The port is explicit: an implementation MUST return `null` — not another tenant's row — when the id exists elsewhere. A scope predicate deleted from a read is a SILENT WIDENING that returns MORE rows and fails no type, which is the shape a suite written by the store's own author is least likely to notice.
kills: an operation id that exists in another tenant reads as null, not as a row
the in-memory double and the PostgreSQL store answer identically

mutations.name: M-P18 operations: updateProgress' ORGANIZATION predicate
mutations.from:
const written = (await transactions.writer(transaction).erasureOperation.updateManyAndReturn({
          where: { id: operationId, organizationId },
mutations.note: The WRITE half of M-P17, and worse: a cross-tenant read returns a row, a cross-tenant WRITE overwrites one. The receipt of one organization's erasure would be advanced by another organization's pass.
kills: an update addressed with the WRONG organization is `not_found`, not a silent no-op

mutations.name: M-P19 operations: listOperationsForSubject's ORGANIZATION predicate
mutations.note: The digests are organization-salted, so a cross-tenant match is improbable rather than impossible — and 'improbable' is not the property the port asks for. This is the read an operator uses as the subject's whole history.
kills: a subject digest that exists in another tenant lists nothing

mutations.name: M-P20 operations: the FREE-LEASE clause of the compare-and-set
mutations.from: OR: [{ leaseExpiresAt: null }, { leaseExpiresAt: { lte: now } }],
mutations.note: THE ONE THE DOUBLE CANNOT SEE. Without this clause every claim wins, so two concurrent resumes both sweep the same subject — and `InMemoryPrivacyRepository` is a map in a single-threaded process, so no suite written against it can lose the race that makes this visible.
kills: two concurrent transactions claim, and precisely one wins
an EXPIRED lease is reclaimable, at the exact instant it lapses
the in-memory double and the PostgreSQL store answer identically

mutations.name: M-P21 operations: the free-lease boundary is <=, not <
mutations.note: `isLeaseFree` is `leaseExpiresAt <= now` — the exact complement of `leaseUntil`, which always returns an instant strictly after `now`. Reversing it leaves a crashed pass's lease held for one extra tick, which is a boundary no wall-clock test can hit and an exact-instant test can.
kills: an EXPIRED lease is reclaimable, at the exact instant it lapses

mutations.name: M-P22 operations: the not-found probe on the lease's LOSING path
mutations.note: Zero affected rows is TWO facts — the lease is held, or the operation is not here — and the port answers them differently: `ok(false)` is a normal outcome and `operationNotFound` is an error. Collapsing them tells a queue that a deleted operation is merely busy, forever.
kills: the in-memory double and the PostgreSQL store answer identically

mutations.name: M-P23 operations: the queue's page is OLDEST DUE FIRST
mutations.note: The port says 'oldest due first'. Reversed, a saturated queue re-drives the newest operations forever and the oldest — the ones that have failed most often — are never reached again.
kills: the in-memory double and the PostgreSQL store answer identically

mutations.name: M-P24 operations: a subject's history is NEWEST FIRST
mutations.note: The port says 'newest first'. An operator reading a subject's history gets the oldest receipt at the top, which for a person erased twice is the one that has since been superseded.
kills: the in-memory double and the PostgreSQL store answer identically
a subject's whole history is ONE statement, for one operation and for twenty-two

mutations.name: M-P25 operations: the unique violation becomes an IDEMPOTENCY CONFLICT
mutations.note: The port REQUIRES the conflict to surface as `PRIVACY_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_CONFLICT`. Rethrown instead, it leaves the port's contract — every method returns a `Result`, a rejected promise is a defect — and a caller racing its own retry sees a driver error rather than the first answer.
kills: a second insert at an occupied key is PRIVACY_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_CONFLICT, naming the winner
a repeated PRIMARY KEY is a DIFFERENT refusal, because there is no winner to name

mutations.name: M-P26 operations: the winner is named from the POOL, not the aborted transaction
mutations.note: `reader()` resolves to the AMBIENT transaction, which is exactly the one PostgreSQL has already aborted with 23505 — so the probe that names the winner is refused with 25P02 rather than answering. This is the one place in this package whose port requires a read to be OUTSIDE the caller's unit of work, and the only reason it is not an escape hatch is that the unit of work is already dead.
kills: a second insert at an occupied key is PRIVACY_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_CONFLICT, naming the winner

mutations.name: M-P27 tombstones: the barrier's read-time expiry
mutations.note: The port: 'a row past its `expiresAt` MUST NOT be returned even when it is still in the table'. Without the clause the barrier refuses writes for a subject whose tombstone lapsed a month ago — an erasure that never ends, for a person who is entitled to be forgotten AND to come back.
kills: a lapsed row is still in the table and is NOT returned
the purge deletes precisely the rows the read already refuses
the in-memory double and the PostgreSQL store answer identically

mutations.name: M-P28 tombstones: read-time expiry is STRICTLY greater
mutations.note: `isActive` is `expiresAt.getTime() > now.getTime()` and `hasElapsed` is its exact complement, so the read rule and the sweep rule cannot disagree about the boundary instant — unless one of them is off by one tick, which is what this is. A row would then be both ACTIVE to the barrier and ELIGIBLE to the purge.
kills: the in-memory double and the PostgreSQL store answer identically

mutations.name: M-P29 tombstones: the barrier's ORGANIZATION predicate
mutations.note: The digests are organization-salted so a cross-tenant match is improbable, and the port's own header says the method is scoped for a SECOND reason as well: 'a method that appeared to allow one would invite an implementation that tried'. This is that implementation.
kills: the in-memory double and the PostgreSQL store answer identically

mutations.name: M-P30 tombstones: the retention sweep's boundary is <=, not <
mutations.note: `hasElapsed` is `!(expiresAt > now)`, so the purge must collect a row whose expiry IS the current instant. One tick out and the sweep leaves behind exactly the rows the read has already stopped honouring — which is harmless for correctness and is the whole reason the two rules are written as complements.
kills: the in-memory double and the PostgreSQL store answer identically

mutations.name: M-P31 tombstones: the EXTEND half of insert-then-extend
mutations.note: A re-seal on retry legitimately creates nothing and must still push the expiry out. Without the extend, a subject sealed on the first pass has their barrier lapse on the ORIGINAL schedule however many times the erasure is retried.
kills: an extend moves the expiry and keeps the row's own identity and seal instant
a seal is THREE statements, for three aliases and for thirty
the in-memory double and the PostgreSQL store answer identically

mutations.name: M-P32 tombstones: the empty alias set costs no statement
mutations.note: Not an optimisation. `guard-subject-write.ts` returns early on an empty set, so the caller that reaches this port with one is the outbox drain's BATCH form — and without the early return every anonymous request in the installation sends `aliasHash IN ()` on the hot path.
kills: an EMPTY alias set costs ZERO statements

mutations.name: M-P33 refusal: the register's outage is its OWN error, not the operation store's
mutations.note: `guard-subject-write.ts` REFUSES A WRITE on `PRIVACY_ERASURE_REGISTER_UNAVAILABLE`, and an operator has to be able to tell 'we blocked a resurrection' from 'we lost the ability to tell'. Two stores sharing one outage code puts both facts under one name on the hot path of every identity chokepoint in the system.
kills: an operation inserted beside a doomed seal does not survive either

mutations.name: M-P34 refusal: a TransactionScopeError is RETHROWN, never folded into a Result
mutations.note: The three scope refusals are the property tranche 1 built and every tranche since has relied on. Folded into a `Result`, a use case that LOST ITS TRANSACTION carries on as though a row had merely failed to write — which in this context means carrying on with a destruction whose barrier is not committed.
kills: a write with NO transaction open is refused `not_open`
a write carrying a FINISHED transaction's token is refused `scope_unknown`
a write carrying ANOTHER LIVE transaction's token is refused `scope_foreign`

survivors.name: S-P01 tombstones: `skipDuplicates: true` on the seal's createMany
note: SURVIVED, AND IS REPORTED RATHER THAN WORKED AROUND. The clause guards a
window this suite cannot produce deterministically: a concurrent seal of the
SAME subject committing between this store's own scoped read and its own
`createMany`. The constraints suite gets as close as a test can — it commits
the winner out of band from INSIDE the loser's transaction — and READ
COMMITTED means the loser's read sees it, so the loser takes the EXTEND
branch and never sends a conflicting INSERT at all. That is exactly why the
case observes `{ sealed: 0, extended: 1 }` and says so.
THE WINDOW IS REAL AND IS MICROSECONDS WIDE. Closing it with a test would
need a fault-injection point inside the store between the two statements,
which would be a seam that exists only for the test. The clause stays, the
mutation is recorded as a survivor, and the case that gets nearest names the
shape it could not reach.

survivors.name: S-P02 tombstones: the `seen` set that mirrors draftTombstones' de-duplication
note: SURVIVED, AND THE REASON IS THAT POSTGRESQL ALREADY HOLDS THE PROPERTY.
`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` skips a row that conflicts with one inserted
earlier in the SAME statement, so a repeated alias in one batch is stored
once and `createMany` reports a count of one either way. The `seen` set is
therefore belt rather than braces here — it keeps the store's own reported
split honest without depending on that behaviour, and it mirrors
`draftTombstones`, which drops a repeated alias before the port is ever
called.
IT IS NOT REMOVED. A guard whose property another layer happens to hold is
not a guard that is doing nothing: the day `skipDuplicates` is reconsidered
(see S-P01) this is what stops one batch aborting the caller's transaction
on its own duplicate.
